title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 106: The Story of Tyrian Purple
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 106 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Story of Tyrian Purple

Paragraph 1. Long before modern factories invented synthetic colours, people in the ancient Mediterranean used colour to display wealth and political authority. The most admired dye was Tyrian purple, named after the Phoenician port city of Tyre in today's Lebanon. Unlike common dyes made from plant roots or crushed insects, Tyrian purple was produced through a difficult process using sea snails from two main species. Fabrics coloured with this rare substance became a proud symbol for kings, priests, and powerful rulers across the region.

Paragraph 2. Producing Tyrian purple was famously slow and disgusting. Sailors caught the snails along rocky coastlines by sinking wicker baskets filled with rotting bait into deep water. Back on land, workers carefully cut out a tiny organ inside large snails using sharp knives, while simply crushing smaller shells completely. The collected liquid was soaked in salt water for three days and then heated slowly inside huge lead containers for ten days. As the mixture boiled, rotting snail tissue released a dreadful stench that spread for miles, forcing towns to keep dye workshops far outside residential neighbourhoods.

Paragraph 3. Sunlight played an essential chemical role in creating the final colour. When first taken from the sea snails, the liquid appeared entirely clear. However, once clean wool was dipped into the warm bath and dried outdoors, direct sunlight triggered a remarkable reaction. Within minutes, the pale cloth shifted through yellow and bright green before turning into a rich, dark purple. Because the dye formed a strong chemical bond with the wool fibres instead of merely sitting on top, regular washing never faded the shade; instead, exposure to sunlight made it even brighter.

Paragraph 4. Due to the tiny amount of liquid inside each snail, Tyrian purple carried an astonishing price. Modern tests show that roughly 10,000 snails were required to produce just a single gram of pure dye powder, making purple cloth as valuable as silver or gold. In Imperial Rome, strict laws controlled who could wear the colour: all-purple robes belonged exclusively to the Emperor, while senior officials could display only a thin purple line along their clothing borders. Roman officers harshly punished traders who sold cheaper fake purple garments coloured with madder root or insects.

Paragraph 5. The ancient dye industry finally collapsed because of major political wars. After the city of Constantinople fell in 1453, the royal workshops that guarded the dye secrets shut down, and the special knowledge disappeared within decades. Purple clothing remained out of reach for ordinary citizens until 1856, when an eighteen-year-old British chemist named William Henry Perkin accidentally created a synthetic purple dye while searching for a malaria medicine. Today, giant piles of ancient discarded snail shells along the Lebanese shoreline still remind visitors of this valuable lost trade.
